messages.author: 6a357ff0681a2a28
messages.subject: Space free on one axis only
parts:
Hi all,

Is there a way to do space free for 1 axis only? Using the dummy plot
code below, you can see that i have a population of 34 animals,
assigned into 2 categories, group X or Y, and 2 measurements A and B
on these animals.

Because group X contains many more animals, the bars per animal are
much more narrow than those of group Y. I therefore used space =
"free", but the problem is that the B measurements are squeezed to
such an extent that the axis and values are not interpretable any
more.

Many thanks in advance!
Best,
tine

####
Animal <- paste("Anim", 1:34, sep = "")
xx <- data.frame(Animal, Value = c(sample(1:10, 17, replace = TRUE),
sample(1:2, 17, replace = TRUE)/5),
group = rep(c(rep("X", 15), rep ("Y", 2)),2), measurement =
c(rep("measurm A",17), rep ("measurm B", 17)), stringsAsFactors =
FALSE)
p <- ggplot(data = xx, aes(x = Animal, y = Value))
p <- p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")
p <- p + facet_grid(measurement ~ group, scales = "free")
p <- p + opts(title = "Option Space Fixed")
print(p)


q <- ggplot(data = xx, aes(x = Animal, y = Value))
q <- q + geom_bar(stat = "identity")
q <- q + facet_grid(measurement ~ group, scales = "free", space =
"free")
q <- q + opts(title = "Option Space Free")
print(q)

parts:
Hi guys,

First of all, thanks for the suggestions. The labels on the X are better like that, but that was not what i am after.

I'll try to explain again. Looking at this plot:

Animal <- paste("Anim", 1:34, sep = "")
xx <- data.frame(Animal, Value = c(sample(1:10, 17, replace = TRUE),
        sample(1:2, 17, replace = TRUE)/5),
    group = rep(c(rep("X", 15), rep ("Y", 2)),2), measurement =
        c(rep("measurm A",17), rep ("measurm B", 17)), stringsAsFactors =
        FALSE)
p <- ggplot(data = xx, aes(x = Animal, y = Value))
p <- p + geom_bar(stat = "identity")
p <- p + facet_grid(measurement ~ group, scales = "free")

print(p)

The scale of the Yaxis is fine (0 -> 10 top and 0 -> 0.4 bottom), but because there are more animals in group X than Y, the difference in width of the bars looks silly. I succeeded in fixing that by adding in space = "free"

q <- ggplot(data = xx, aes(x = Animal, y = Value))
q <- q + geom_bar(stat = "identity")
q <- q + facet_grid(measurement ~ group, scales = "free", space = "free")

print(q)

However for this plot, the Y axis are scaled too, so that the bottom plot is squeezed. 

Ideally i would like the X axis of the 2nd plot and the Y axis of the 1st one. Which is why i was wondering if it is possible to get space = "free_x" and not for Y in this case.

Thanks again,

tine

If you want independent scales in each facet, you're going to have to
use another approach. For example, you could make four independent
plots and then render them in a 2 x 2 arrangement using the grid
package and its layout features. [You need grid because ggplot2 is
based on grid graphics.] An alternative is to use the grid.arrange()
function in the gridExtra package. The example below uses the former
approach, illustrated on p. 154 of the ggplot2 book.

Moreover, I'm wondering why you would want to use a bar chart to plot
values. Bar charts are intended to visualize discrete distributions -
any other use of that visual metaphor is, IMO, senseless. It wastes
ink and obscures patterns. Why aren't you using line plots for this
instead? They consume less ink and do a better job of telling the
story (i.e., they have a higher information-to-ink ratio). Here's one
way to do it. I chose to split the data frames so that there was one
data frame per plot, but strictly speaking, this isn't necessary.

# This violates the DRY principle (don't repeat yourself)
# I'm making an exception for this purpose
ds1 <- subset(xx, group == 'X' & measurement == 'measurm A')
ds2 <- subset(xx, group == 'X' & measurement == 'measurm B')
ds3 <- subset(xx, group == 'Y' & measurement == 'measurm A')
ds4 <- subset(xx, group == 'Y' & measurement == 'measurm B')

# Create a numeric vector to use as the x-axis values in each plot
ds1$anim <- seq_len(nrow(ds1))
ds2$anim <- seq_len(nrow(ds2))
ds3$anim <- seq_len(nrow(ds3))
ds4$anim <- seq_len(nrow(ds4))

p1 <- ggplot(ds1, aes(anim, Value)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
labs(x = '') + ylim(0, 10) +
opts(title = 'Gp: X Meas: A',
plot.title = theme_text(size = 10)) +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = ds1$anim,
labels = sapply(ds1$Animal, function(s) substr(s, 5, 6)))
p2 <- ggplot(ds2, aes(anim, Value)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = ds2$anim,
labels = sapply(ds2$Animal, function(s) substr(s, 5, 6))) +
labs(x = 'Animal') + ylim(0, 0.4) +
opts(title = 'Gp: X Meas: B',
axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 9),
plot.title = theme_text(size = 10))
p3 <- ggplot(ds3, aes(anim, Value)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = ds3$anim,
labels = sapply(ds3$Animal, function(s) substr(s, 5, 6))) +
labs(x = "", y = "") + ylim(0, 10) +
opts(title = 'Gp: Y Meas: A',
axis.text.y = theme_blank(),
plot.title = theme_text(size = 10),
plot.background = theme_blank())
p4 <- ggplot(ds4, aes(anim, Value)) + geom_point() + geom_line() +
scale_x_continuous(breaks = ds4$anim,
labels = sapply(ds4$Animal, function(s) substr(s, 5, 6))) +
labs(x = 'Animal', y = "") + ylim(0, 0.4) +
opts(title = 'Gp: Y Meas: B',
plot.title = theme_text(size = 10),
axis.text.y = theme_blank(),
axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 9),
plot.background = theme_blank())

library('grid')

vplayout <- function(x, y)
viewport(layout.pos.row = x, layout.pos.col = y)

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(100, 100)))

print(p1, vp = vplayout(1:50, 1:85))
print(p3, vp = vplayout(1:50, 81:100))
print(p2, vp = vplayout(51:100, 1:85))
print(p4, vp = vplayout(51:100, 81:100))


Alternatively, you could order the animals by increasing value if that
was meaningful - the simplest way to do this would be to add a
character variable to each of the split data frames corresponding to
the animal number as I did in the sapply() function, use the arrange()
function in plyr or order() in base to order the rows by value and
then plot.

It's not necessary to split the data frames as I did here - you could
do all this in the plyr package with a little effort and then use
subset() for the individual plots. Because you wanted different x/y
scales in different panels, you have to go this route.

I inserted enough elements here for you to play with and tweak to your choice.

HTH,
Dennis

> Moreover, I'm wondering why you would want to use a bar chart to plot

> any other use of that visual metaphor is, IMO, senseless. It wastes

> instead? They consume less ink and do a better job of telling the
> story (i.e., they have a higher information-to-ink ratio). Here's one
> way to do it. I chose to split the data frames so that there was one

> ds2 <- subset(xx, group == 'X' & measurement == 'measurm B')
